title: A Tibetan day

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bardo, the in-between after death, and in every gap of life. Your line: in between. Today, the last day of the diamond vehicle.

Early morning in a Tibetan settlement in India. A grandmother wakes before her family, washes her face, and fills seven small bowls with water on the family shrine. She lights a lamp and bows three times. Then she walks to the temple with her beads, joining a slow river of people circling it clockwise, murmuring, turning the prayer wheels as they pass. Later she'll sit for a while at home. None of it is dramatic. All of it has a shape.
screen: `SEVEN BOWLS OF WATER.` → `A LAMP, THREE BOWS.` → `CIRCLING THE TEMPLE WITH BEADS.`

segments.voice: Tibetan teachers often say a practice should be good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good at the end. It begins with refuge: turning toward the Buddha, the teaching and the community, and in Tibetan practice often the teacher too. Right after comes bodhicitta, the reminder of why: for all beings. Many people say a short traditional verse joining the two, three times. The middle is the practice itself: om mani padme hum on the beads, a praise to Tara, a visualization, or tonglen, riding the breath. Whatever it is, teachers say to do it without grabbing at results. The end is dedication. Whatever good came from this is given away, to all beings, so it can't turn into a private trophy. A ten-minute session and a three-year retreat share that same shape. Around it sits the rest of the day: water bowls and lamps, the walk around the temple, the wheels, the flags on the roof. Now look back at two weeks on the roof of the world. The diamond vehicle. The jewel in the lotus. The wind carries it. Turn the mind. Check the teacher. Take in, send out. One slogan. For all of us. She comes quickly. Swept away. Four streams. Carried into exile. In between. And today, the diamond day. Tomorrow the path comes down from the mountains, to wherever you live, with a practical question: who will you practice with?
screen: `BEGINNING: REFUGE AND BODHICITTA.` · `MIDDLE: MANTRA, TARA, TONGLEN.` · `END: GIVE THE GOOD AWAY.` · `WATER BOWLS, LAMPS, THE TEMPLE WALK.` · then, large: `THE DIAMOND DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the shape in miniature: begin by turning silently toward what you take refuge in, and remember you're not sitting only for yourself. In the middle, sit with the breath, or murmur om mani padme hum if that feels right, without chasing any result. At the end, give it away, whatever good came from this, for all beings; another day, the same shape can stretch to fifteen minutes.
A Tibetan day. Refuge and bodhicitta at the start, mantra or tonglen in the middle, and dedication at the end: good in the beginning, middle and end.
Your line: the diamond day. Good in the beginning, the middle and the end. Two weeks on the mountain, complete.
